objectives: Compare malaria and dengue agents and vectors.
Connect life cycles and vector ecology with prevention.
prerequisites: A vector is distinct from the agent it transmits.
Viruses and protozoan parasites are different biological groups.

terms.Plasmodium: A genus of protozoan parasites that includes malaria agents.
terms.biological vector: A living transmitter in which an agent undergoes relevant development or replication.
terms.viraemia: Presence of virus in the blood.

conceptualTeaching.explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites, commonly transmitted through infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Parasites introduced during a bite undergo liver stages before blood-stage parasites infect red blood cells. Repeated multiplication and release from red cells contribute to illness; some sexual forms can be taken up by another mosquito, completing transmission. The parasite is not a bacterium, and the mosquito is not the human liver stage. Exact fever timing is not a reliable universal diagnostic rule.

Dengue is viral and is principally transmitted by infected Aedes mosquitoes. The virus replicates in the human host and vector as part of its transmission cycle; it does not follow the Plasmodium liver-to-red-cell protozoan cycle. Dengue can range in severity, and some cases involve serious plasma leakage or bleeding-related complications. Fever alone cannot distinguish it from malaria or other infections. Use agent and vector evidence, not the generic phrase mosquito disease, to explain the difference.

Reducing mosquito breeding sites, limiting bites and organized vector control can interrupt transmission. Measures must fit the vector’s habitats and biting behaviour; bed nets are important in relevant malaria settings, while avoiding daytime Aedes exposure and container breeding can matter for dengue. These are complementary ecological controls, not a claim that one intervention guarantees elimination. Vaccine or drug eligibility and current recommendations vary and need current public-health guidance; this lesson does not invent a universal schedule or shared treatment.

nodes: Malaria: Anopheles → Plasmodium liver stage → red-cell stages → mosquito
Dengue: Aedes → dengue virus in host → mosquito
visualUnderstanding.description: Draw parallel labelled transmission loops with agent names and vector names in separate boxes.
visualUnderstanding.limitations: Qualitative routes; no epidemiological prediction, fever-based diagnosis or treatment selection.

realWorldApplication.example: Two mosquito-control campaigns may need different timing and habitat priorities because the vectors are not biologically identical.

examinationApplication.prompt: Compare malaria and dengue with reference to agent, vector, mechanism and prevention.

questions.prompt: Which pairing and human-stage sequence is correct for malaria?

options.A: Aedes → Plasmodium → red-cell stages before the initial liver stage.
options.B: Anopheles → Plasmodium → liver stages followed by red-cell stages.
options.C: Anopheles → dengue virus → liver stages followed by red-cell stages.
options.D: Aedes → dengue virus → the Plasmodium sexual cycle in human red cells.

optionExplanations.A: This swaps the principal vector and broad initial human sequence.
optionExplanations.B: Correct principal malaria vector, agent and human-stage order.
optionExplanations.C: This substitutes dengue virus for the malaria parasite.
optionExplanations.D: It combines different agents and misplaces the Plasmodium sexual cycle.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason not to treat malaria and dengue as one disease?

options.A: They always involve identical vectors and human stages.
options.B: They can be distinguished reliably from fever timing alone.
options.C: They differ in causal agent, vector relationships and pathogenesis.
options.D: All vector-control measures have identical effectiveness against both.

optionExplanations.A: Their agent–vector relationships and mechanisms differ.
optionExplanations.B: Symptoms and timing alone are not universal identification rules.
optionExplanations.C: The mechanistic differences require distinct explanations.
optionExplanations.D: Ecology and behaviour influence the suitability of each measure.

answerWriting.modelResponse: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Its human cycle includes liver stages followed by red-cell infection and multiplication. Dengue is caused by dengue virus and is principally transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; it does not have the same protozoan red-cell cycle. Both can cause fever, so symptoms alone cannot establish the agent. Prevention combines vector-source management and suitable bite reduction, adapted to the relevant mosquito ecology. A comparison diagram should separate agent, vector and human stages and avoid proposing one universal treatment.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identify the malaria agent and vector.
Correctly identify dengue as viral and Aedes-associated.
Explain why shared fever does not establish shared cause.

commonMistakes: Using mosquito as the name of the pathogen.
